newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan output data dampens rate hike expectations.
newsitem.headline: Japan output data dampens rate hike expectations.

text.p: Japan's industrial production figure for April showed an unexpected decline on Thursday, dampening market expectations of an early interest rate increase based on a brighter economic outlook.

"For the markets, the message should be very simple and straightforward: This number underscores that the Bank of Japan (BOJ) is not going to be in a hurry to hike interest rates in the next three to six months," Jesper Koll, head of research at J.P. Morgan, Tokyo, told Reuters Financial Television (RFTV).

According to data released by Japan's Ministry of International Trade and Industry (MITI), Japan's April industrial output fell a preliminary 0.4 percent from the previous month on a seasonally adjusted basis.

A MITI official told reporters that output in the April-to-June period was expected to fall 0.7 percent from the previous quarter, although compared with the same period a year ago, it would register a gain of 6.1 percent.
The official attributed the dip in production in April to a rise in Japan's sales tax to five percent from three percent on April 1 and to a slip in production from orders.

Financial markets responded quickly to the weaker-than-expected data, with Euroyen futures, the dollar and Japanese government bonds all leaping on the news, as expectations of an early Japanese rate rise faded.
Currency traders said that the dollar rose to about 116.48 yen in afternoon Tokyo trade as the yield of Japanese government bonds kept slipping after the data.

The market had been speculating that an early rise in the Japan's official discount rate was possible after the Bank of Japan said late on Wednesday that it would release its next "tankan" survey of corporate sentiment on June 25, rather than in early July.
The central bank has kept the discount rate -- that at which it lends to commercial banks -- at a record-low 0.5 percent since September 1995, in an effort to stimulate economic recovery.
Despite the markets' reaction to Thursday's data, some economists doubted whether expectations of a rate hike had competely disappeared.

"There's no change in the fact that the BOJ will change its monetary policy somewhere along the line and it's hard to imagine that expectations of a rate hike will recede drastically just with the industrial output data," said Yukinobu Kaibe, manager of the treasury planning division at Nippon Credit Bank.
"The movement (in Euroyen and bonds) is more like a technical one," Masanobu Takahashi, director and head of research at Sanyo Investment Research, told RFTV.
"Although a shocking figure for traders, it'll soon subside when the production figures for May and June and the quarterly numbers come out."

MITI said in a statement on Thursday that although industrial production had slowed for temporary reasons, it continues to rise strongly in year-on-year terms and is on a gradual rising trend in general.

Yukio Yambe, chief economist at DKB Research Institute Corp, said that a rise in inventories hinted at a possible downward revision of MITI's forecast for May data, but overall, industrial output is relatively solid and is still on an increasing trend.
"There's a possibility that the BOJ may raise the official discount rate by 0.5 percentage point if they confirm strong May production data as expected," Yambe said.

On Wednesday, BOJ Governor Yasuo Matsushita repeated his oft-heard saying that the central bank will continue to carry out a monetary policy that emphasises strengthening the basis of the economic recovery. This is taken to mean the bank will stick with its policy of low interest rates for the time being.
